utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here from the defence teams. I just notice the absence of Mr. Haynes and Mr. Krgovic. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey, back in form, and Mr. Mitchell. The witness is here. Good morning to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to continue and hopefully finish soon. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Colonel, good morning.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: With some trepidation, I take you back to the water system. One of the -- Ms. Faveau wanted a document that she found, and it's a document that helps finish up that chapter, so if we could go to 65 ter 3501, and I'll show you. I'm not supposed to hands you things directly. I'm not sure how much more we have to say about this, but we can see this is a 21 June 1993 document, and if you remember where we left off with the water system, we had a 21 June document requesting for a report of the barbaric acts about the water system, and if we look at this it seems to be just that: A report about the Muslim attack on the water system. Interestingly, you can be -- it can be seen in the top of this document in the handwritten version that it says -- well, it says personally to the Drina Corps commander, and then it says to the GSVRS, personally to General Milovanovic, forwarded at 2340 hours. And we all know that at the time, General Milovanovic was the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff. And we can see from looking at this document, for example, on the third paragraph from the end, Vukota Vukovic actually goes and talks to a major from the Canada battalion. Says on 27 May, "The following day during the meeting with the UNPROFOR I protested with the major from K Canada saying that they served as a shield to the Muslim terrorist to destroy the facilities without disturbances only to accuse us before the world for the so-called vandalism, just like they always do. We couldn't have directed the focus of fire towards this stretch checkpoint river Zeleni Jadar because we didn't want to endanger the UNPROFOR forces which were located at the observation point and which they saw for themselves. They replied positively to my claims, disgusted by the Muslim's behaviour." Well, this is isn't new in any kind of military, is it, to blame the other side for doing bad things and to present yourself in the world as the great conquerer or the great military force. I mean, we see that when we turn on CNN today. So there's nothing all that unusual about this, is there? How do you react to this? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in view of the fact that in the materials during my preparations preparing my expert report, I came across statements made previously prior to the completion of my report, and among them there were a lot of them, but I did not find a single trace of what I see before me now. So I have no more in-depth knowledge about this. I have what I'm seeing now, and it is my opinion that this action as described here for the place role and tasks which the people performed is, first of all, outside the functions or remit of security, and the idea of it is very unclear to me in any way. If all these are facts which are correct, then it is my opinion that this action goes beyond the tasks assigned within the Drina Corps zone to the units that executed tasks and what I had to study. This goes beyond that; it's outside that area. So that's all I can say because you would need to have an in-depth analysis of all this, and as a security expert myself, I would like to say that there are things that remain unclear from the idea of the action itself, then allowing it to go ahead and all the rest of it. It goes beyond that area. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down a little bit, Colonel, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, one last question on this, and we'll let the water system go. I'm sure you have read and you have heard in the media as we all have of -- well, first of all of what the BiH and the Muslim army talks about their oppressed situation, but that's not what I want to ask you about. We constantly hear from the Serbian media, from the VRS that they are being treated unfairly by the world; they are portrayed -- the VRS or the RS or Serbia has been portrayed as some sort of villainous group, and that they are being treated unfairly. Isn't this operation as we see it unfolding doing just that, trying to portray the VRS in this context as being the victims of terrorism and thereby putting out to the world that they are the victims when in reality they have created the action and they have manufactured this for world consumption?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like my learned friend to tell us who the "they" is, which media, what period of time he is referring to, what are the grounds for this type of question, and what is the object of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Again, we are pretty much in the same waters as we were yesterday when we told you we can draw our own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this document that we've just seen that was offered by Ms. Faveau exposes the myth of Serbian victimisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's an argument. Stop. Stop. Stop. That's an argument. This is a precisely what I was try to convey to you, that but let me consult with my colleagues first to make sure that they are in agreement with me before ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to say that this is precisely the document that I wanted to cross-examine upon. Indeed, I'm not quite sure that it was properly interpreted by Mr. McCloskey within the context of other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. With a 2:1 majority, let's move on to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to another document, Colonel. It's 65 ter number 453, and let me give you a Serbian version that you'll see a little highlight on. This is a document dated 17 July and is signed by the UNPROFOR, the Muslim representative, and Miroslav Deronjic. And it talks about on 12 July in the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac, "At our request negotiations were conducted between the representatives of our civilian authorities and the representatives of the Republika Srpska civilian authorities, and the army regarding the evacuation of our civilian population from the Srebrenica enclaves." Gives the names of the representatives, says from our side, and it's the Muslims. Then it says the people from the Serbian side, and we can see Deronjic and Mladic and some people from the Bratunac municipality. And it goes on, and we can see General Krstic, Bosic, and then it says chief of the corps security, Mr. Popovic, and Colonel Kosovic. Where does being a representative in a situation like this fit into the job of Drina Corps security? But -- I'm sorry, let me first ask you. Have you had a chance to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I read this document during the preparation of my expert report, so I do know; I am familiar with its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then can you tell us how, if it does, would this particular task that he was engaged in on the 12th of July that is reflected in this document, how does that fit into his job as the Drina Corps chief of security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, an answer was provided to that question in the expert report. In the part relating to Judas, the operative action, and the additional dossier for the protection of General Mladic from the ordered killing was in the Drina Corps command in the security department, or more specifically, it was with Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. And with respect to that action, he had to be engaged directly in the area and along the facilities where at that point in time Ratko Mladic was located when the risk existed which could lead to the implementation of this order issued or this killing that was commissioned. So he had to coordinate broader security directly as well as counterintelligence with -- by -- and provide direct security. Nobody else could do that instead of him in that place and at that time, and that is why he happened to be there, not as a member of the delegation for negotiations but in his capacity as a security organ and the protagonist, the sole protagonist of the job in hand with respect to the Judas operative action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did he tell you that, or are you just gleaning that from your knowledge of the regulations and the materials you've looked at?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I spent my entire career working on operative actions and things connected to them. The documents that I had in my hands without a doubt speak to the fact that there was information upon which the security organs of the Army Republika Srpska in every section of area under their authority had to react --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: -- without reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to go to a few paragraphs in your report, which would be 65 ter number 1D1175, page 20 in the English, page 18 in the B/C/S. I want to give to you the portions of the report so you can read it. It starts on Section 2.116, and just to start off with, these are paragraphs that I actually agree with you on but I just want to ask you a couple of things about. So just to start off with, if we look at section 2.116, you cite the instructions on the use of the service regulations of the military police, and you state "The military police provide security only for certain categories of prisoners of war and when this is ordered by a special order." And then you go on to explain in paragraph 2.117, "This refers only to certain categories of prisoners of war or, concretely, to important prisoners of war. That is not a regular prescribed duty of the military police but a special case. It should be noted that only the commander of the unit in which the military police unit is placed or a person authorised by him may issue an order for the military police to provide security for prisoners of war." And then if we go on in your report to paragraph 4.30, which is on page 47 in the English, and page 39 of the B/C/S, you say: "Prisoners of war and war booty are not a threat to security in the Drina Corps zone in such a way or to such an extent as to require the engagement of the most professional part of the security system for this task." So these -- well, on the 13th, 14th of July, these thousands of Muslims, if they were to just be shipped up for exchange really didn't present the kind of security issue that would require the time and effort of, as you say, the most professional part of the security system, Popovic, Beara?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: This question demands a fuller explanation because it's a simplistic view if we compare it to the problems that existed in the zone of deployment of the prisoners of war. We are not dealing here with a threat itself, a threat from the prisoners of war or the threat that the prisoners of war might have presented. What we are dealing here is a security situation in the area of the brigade in which there were a large number of armed people and a certain number of infiltrated armed groups in the rear, and they had the task and, indeed, the ability, and we saw that they were interested in the places of incarceration, and they had the possibility -- or, rather, because not sufficient security could be provided for the prisoners of war, they could have been liberated. So one had to assess all the possibilities to hand, and another one -- there was a very realistic threat, as well, and that was that through the corridor in other ways arms could be infiltrated to those who had been released, and then the balance of forces would have been upset in the area of responsibility of the brigade, so much so that the defence of the zone was no longer tenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So are you saying we can expect that Colonel Beara would be directly interested in all these prisoners to be present in and around them? Are you now -- is that what you are now testifying to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: What I want to say is what I in fact said, and that is that the danger was a serious one and that as such it demanded that all possibilities be dealt with to prevent this development of events. Now, to what extent that was the role of the security organs to provide, this was decided among other things, by the command that had its assessments and decided on the basis of those assessments how to react, what steps were to be taken; and from the work that I had in hand, I found that the situation was as we see in a document a borderline case that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not a borderline case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but that it was on the brink of catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you stand by your statement in paragraph 4.30, that the prisoners of war and war booty are not a threat to the security of the Drina Corps zone in such a way or such an extent as to require the engagement of the most professional part of the security system for this task? The key part of that is "require the engagement of". Does what you are talking about require the engagement of the security people, Beara, Popovic and others?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I answered very precisely. I said why the danger existed, and it absolutely coincides with this assertion made in this paragraph of the report. They coincide fully, not because I wanted that to be the case but because the actual situation was such. The danger wasn't from the prisoners of war themselves and of themselves, but the danger came from the fact that for the -- there was interest in the prisoners of war being released and then as military able men to be transported to territory under the control of the Muslim forces and to be dealt with further as military able males, men, when the general mobilisation was proclaimed in the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the crux of the matter and the substance of my answer as to what dangers existed and what threats existed, so there is a clear delineation between the prisoners of war themselves per se and the fact that there was the -- a danger looming. That is to say that they would be released and then would even be provided with weapons. So that was the problem, the security problem that had to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So are you now saying that the danger that the Muslims would be released was to the extent that it would require the engagement of the most professional part of the security system?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I did not directly participate or observe. I was merely an analyst trying to see all of the facts objectively so as to arrive at a conclusion, and that conclusion is contained in the document. The conclusion was that the threat, the danger was such that the situation was at the brink of disaster, and I cannot interpret it in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll try one more time. Colonel, you say in this document, in your report that this threat would not require the engagement of the most professional part of the security system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this particular part of report is related just to one particular document, not for all events, not for all events, but Mr. McCloskey presented --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a very nice answer for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. You took just one part -- just one page of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, stop. Please, let's keep -- stick to the basic rules of procedure. No cross-table argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can move on to a related but similar area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Colonel, in your view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. May we provide the witness with his report? His binder -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was under the impression that he had his two binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He had it yesterday, but he was not able to find anything in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yeah, but it's fair enough. He should have -- he should have the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course. Now he can refer to the document you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, it should be page 18 in the B/C/S for those first two things and page 39 in the B/C/S on that last part that I read to you. Section -- paragraph 4.30. And the question I want to ask for you now is that -- I think I understand your answer, so was it more important in your view based on the documents and the materials of this case that Beara and Popovic were present in and around these thousands of prisoners; it was more important for them to be there with them than it would be taking part in providing operational security and other important counterintelligence matters and the ongoing operations of Zepa and the areas -- and the Krajina and other secure areas, areas of security issues?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was about to answer your question previously, which had to do with some additional circumstances and insight they had, which now I cannot interpret from the point of view of importance. A decision on the situation and the importance and urgency is made by a person directly involved. An expert cannot offer his interpretation on the circumstances involved. He can only draw conclusions based on the documents received. Therefore, what I can tell you is that, yes, there was something or, no, there wasn't, but that would be speculation. I'm not here to speculate. What I conclude on the basis of this is that the events were very traumatic. This is what we find in the documents and from the situation in the field. This is what I based and formulated my conclusion on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So based on everything you've looked at, you conclude that it would be more important for Beara and Popovic to be around these prisoners than doing their security job in Zepa or the Krajina or wherever else security issues arose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question has already been asked and I believe answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with half of that, but I don't think he has gotten anywhere near an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we agree with you. We are perfectly in agreement with you. Colonel, could you answer the question in a complete manner, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm responsible here as an expert. I cannot tell you whether for Beara and Popovic it was more important for them to be there than to deal with certain other tasks. It was their assessment, their decision, and I do not want to speculate. That is all I have to say. As for the rest of what I said, I observed the facts and I based my conclusions on them as well as my assessment, and I offered my view and my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a very simple question, Colonel. Based on everything you have read and according -- you've been giving opinions all throughout your five days of defence testimony, was from your knowledge of the documents was the -- their need, was it greater in the Zvornik area or in the Bratunac area around the prisoners or the need that you understood for operational security for Zepa and the other security matters, and I would ask the Court to order him to answer that particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's keep it cool. I mean, don't take that -- we know when to intervene, and we do. Colonel, please, could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can only repeat what I've said. These decisions were made by the officers tasked with making those decisions. I don't know what my position would have been had I been in their shoes, but from this position I don't have the insight into the security situation in other parts of the area. However, the fact remains that the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade was overburdened by serious security issues, and the role of the security organs was to do their utmost in order to avoid any loss of control in the area of the Zvornik Brigade, and that must have been more important than going to some other areas where the security in question was in less of a danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel. Now, you've talked a lot about the importance of operational security. We've seen in the Drina Corps plans and other plans how important secrecy was for these military operations to keep the VRS intentions away from the enemy, away from the public; and you've emphasized that this was an important part of the security officer's job. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, and it was ordered by the command structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. And so the best professional minds and officers for operational security in the VRS should have been Tolimir; Beara; and for the Drina Corps, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic; and for the Zvornik Brigade, Drago Nikolic; and for the Bratunac Brigade, Momir Nikolic, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. McCloskey. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, the military prosecutors office of the VRS talked about potential crimes against humanity and war crimes and that -- acknowledged that that could happen in any war. And I want to ask you - and we don't need to put this to the VRS; let's say VRS, maybe BiH - but if the ruling commanders in either of those armies made the horrific decision to murder many hundreds of prisoners in an operation that would involve detention, transportation, execution, and burial, what branch of the military service would best serve the operational security of such an operation that needed to be done quickly, quietly, and efficiently?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: When secret operations of the service are involved, that's what I can talk about. As regards the planning of such activities, it would indeed entail the existence of a secret way to carry out those tasks. As for the service itself or any service, for that matter, it could not have been handled by one service alone because this goes beyond the measures of security and secrecy involved. It begins with the plan and all of its elements and implementation as intended. That is why I cannot weigh that as to -- or assign it to any particular service. In any case, if such a plan were to take place, each of the participants would have to have a clearly defined role in this secret operation. It is impossible for one side to protect the secrecy of the operation without all the other elements being fully acquainted with it. That is what I can say about planning and secrecy in terms of operations. As for the service, the counterintelligence aspect of it, that is what I can address in detail. Otherwise, all I can say is that it is a very sensitive, encompassing plan to do something of this scale secretly. It cannot be done by a single service alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Zivanovic, do you have redirect, or Ms. Nikolic? Do you have, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have as well. Okay. Ms. Faveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before my colleagues start this additional cross-examination, I would like to ask your leave to put a few questions that come directly from the cross-examination we've just had by the Prosecution. The fact, for example, that the Prosecutor used the document that I said I would like to use proves that this is essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't let him use that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Faveau, you remember what we had said at the beginning when we were approaching the beginning of the Defence case, namely that we would take this on a case-by-case basis. We wouldn't like to see it happening on a regular basis. Before taking a decision, we would like to know what the questions are, and then we'll decide. I know that yesterday you indicated that you had three documents that you meant to make use of, two of which we are aware of, the other one we haven't seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two documents on the water tower and the aqueduct, and I would like to prove that the dates do not correspond and that the interpretation of the Prosecutor may be faulty. The third document is a document sent by General Tolimir to General Miletic, and I only have two questions on this document. First question is, who could approve General Tolimir's proposal; and the second question is as far as the witness knows whether these proposals were adopted and the actions undertaken on the basis of those proposals made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, can you take off your headphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I'll stay out of the water system controversy, but those last two issues could very well have been brought up on cross. I don't -- by herself. I don't see -- you know, they are short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but the question had not arisen during -- had it arisen during the direct? Yes, Ms. Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was a document that was absolutely new, that had not been used during the in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am under the impression that was used by Mr. Zivanovic, actually. Wasn't it? The letter from Tolimir to Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure which document she means, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand you and her, actually, because once you eliminated the water tank, then you were necessarily talking about the letter from Tolimir to Miletic. That's how I understand it, anyway. That matter was raised by you on cross-examination and not by Mr. Zivanovic during direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We still haven't found that, and I'm sure you are right, SO if that's the case ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document P2517. This is a document dated July 21st from General Tolimir and dealing with Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, and we are in agreement that that was used during cross-examination and not during the direct, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And of course, that document has been used many, many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will then object to the violation of the rules. Let's stick by the rules we've been living by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. What we are going to suggest for the time being is that we proceed with the redirect of Ms. Nikolic; and during the break, Ms. Faveau, see if you can discuss a little bit with your two colleagues, Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Zivanovic, and see if they can take on board your queries, which would save us having to find a legal formula either to accept or reject your request to put further questions to the witness. Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you necessary to clarify a few things after the cross-examination by my learned friend. In your yesterday's testimony, you were asked by Mr. Haynes at page 23359 of the transcript. You were talking about when the military police can be used outside of the scope of their tasks and competences. When the military police is used in such a way, on the approval of the army commander or another senior officer in such a case, does the army commander or the senior officer can issue an order directly to the security organ circumventing the unit commander, the part of whose unit the military police unit is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The regulation that there is does not envisage such a possibility that the security organ can be issued orders by the second or two levels up in terms of command because the military police is under the command of the commander of the unit, the part of which that military police unit is. When commanding the military unit, a request needs to come down the chain of command. This is what the regulation requests, and only in very exceptional circumstances can such a circumvention take place. However, in my career I have not come across such an example. It would have been a precedent. That is why we have the regular way of communication prescribed by the regulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sending the military police into combat, does that fall within the remit and tasks of the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: If you read the documents carefully, you can see straight away in the reports that it says the military police tasks, and then they are enumerated; the military police tasks are set out, and then as a separate part it says participation in combat operations. So the military police does not take part in combat operations when it comes to its remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if the military police is nonetheless used in combat, in combat operations, who decides on the deployment of the military police in combat operations and whether the security organ is consulted in making that decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. I don't recall dealing in these details with the military police, and combat is something that was dealt with on cross in any detail, and if it had been it's already been dealt with. It's just fundamental material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if I remember, I may be wrong, but if I remember well, during the examination-in-chief by Mr. Zivanovic, he was even shown the provision of the law which precisely deals with the deployment of military police in combat operations, and the questions were asked to whom, who would decide certain questions, certain issues, and who would decide others and to whom they were answerable. So I think we can safely move to your next question, Ms. Nikolic. Unless I am wrong, but I think the Colonel himself can confirm this. You have already been asked about this, haven't you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was asked questions about that and it was discussed, although I wasn't able to see what else there was in the question, so that's the crux of the matter just as you noted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd just like to ask one sentence, the basis for my additional questions as to the deployment of the military police outside the purview, its purview, based on special orders, and this was raised by my colleagues during the cross-examination, and I think that sending the military police into combat operations is one type of task of this kind, and I'd like to clear that up with the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was not something that I brought up. I brought up special use of the military police with prisoners, special orders related to prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I mentioned Mr. Zivanovic because it was Mr. Zivanovic who dealt with the deployment of military personnel, military police, and security personnel in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to page 23360 of the transcript and 23361. 23360 and 23361 of the 7th of July, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She is referring to what -- to a part during Mr. Haynes' cross-examination. Given that, we allow the question. So please, Colonel, Ms. Nikolic is going to put the question to you, which I understand is a prelude to another question or series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question, Colonel, if you need to hear it again. My question was as follows: The security organ, does it decide whether the military police will be deployed in combat operations, or is it the commander who decides having consulted the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: When it comes to the engagement of the military police in combat, combat operations, there is no role there played by the security organ because it goes beyond the remit and function of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In case the military police is sent in to combat operations, does the security organ follow the unit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The security organ in the professional sense manages the military police only when a military police unit is deployed within the frameworks of the prescribed remit, that is to say, is within military police tasks and assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go back to another area now. Yesterday on the 7th of July, you also testified on pages 23363 and 23364 of the transcript for my colleagues. Actually, you were shown your findings in the Vukovar case. So I'd like to ask us to have on e-court 7D952, pages 29 and 30 of those findings. 29 and 30 of the B/C/S, in fact, and it is page 30 in the English. May we scroll down for the B/C/S, please. Lower down the page. Thank you. On the right-hand side we have the B/C/S version, and the last sentence says that the infantry brigade and the military police is subordinated to the commander of the brigade. Now, can we have page 30 in B/C/S, and it's the same page in English. The military police company commander subordinated the brigade commander indirectly, et cetera, i.e., via the chief of the security organ of the brigade who is leading the military police in the professional sense. And I'd also like to read out on that same page, 30 of the B/C/S, the second paragraph, third sentence, in an infantry brigade the security organ is an intermediary through which the brigade commander manages and commands the military police in all aspects and in all contents. Mr. Vuga, my question to you is this: Compared to your findings and the expert report in this trial and in the Vukovar trial, are there any substantive or other differences in these observations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mrs. Nikolic, in the proceedings we are discussing there was a comparative analysis that was made of one type of infantry brigade and the motorised guard's brigade, which was a specific unit in all respects. So this type of infantry brigade displayed this type of control and command of the military police, but it was not absolute because there were other ways of control which were not excluded in this type of brigade, which means there was no substantive difference between what is stated in my expert report in this trial and in the previous trial that we are discussing at present.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to have on e-court another document or, rather, the same document, 7D952, but I'd like to see the schematic, the diagram that we were discussing yesterday. So first of all, I'd like to ask that page 88 be displayed in English and page 91 in the B/C/S of this document 7D952. Thank you. Colonel, the diagram that we have in front of us contains -- or shows the links, the linkup between the units, and there are full lines and dotted lines. Now, what I want to ask you is this: The dotted lines on this diagram, which emerge from the security organ and the military police department going down towards the other segments, that dotted line, does that reflect professional management or command in the sense that you testified about here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mrs. Nikolic, a comparative analysis or comparisons generally of the guards motorised brigade with other brigades cannot provide us with the proper solution because the motorised guards brigade was a specific units of the Yugoslav People's Army, and in the case of that unit the manner of control and command are not comparable to a classical infantry brigade of the kind we have studied thus far.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, may we have B/C/S page 93 and the English, which is the same page of that same document. I'm sorry. I apologise. The page in English is page 90. Colonel, you were asked yesterday about this schematic of the composition of the infantry brigade from the Vukovar report. Now, the dotted line there between the upper two rectangles, does that denote some form of control and command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: It is neither in this particular case. This is a type of cooperation, and this dotted line where it says SKJ Committee can be struck from the agenda because as it stands, it no longer existed either within the JNA later nor within the Army of Republika Srpska, so that rectangle does not deserve any more extensive comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So your diagram in this trial is different than it is in your expert report in the Popovic et al trial?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, the function is different as is shown here, and it is individual. It doesn't coincide with others.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: May we have on e-court the next exhibit, please. It is 3D396. The B/C/S page is 40, and it is 48 in English. This is a schematic of the report that you compiled in the trial you are testifying in today. We have dotted lines once again and lines linking certain participants, factors, according to the military police company, the security organs, and further down -- who else? So what do the dotted lines further down represent?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner, you have the key, and it says that the dotted lines are specialist control, it says, or professional management. And they are lines of the chief of the security organs, which denote professional management and guidance. The military police company through the commander of the military police company and professional management and guidance in the security and intelligence organs within the battalions, assistant commanders for security in the battalions, which come under the authority of the chief of the security organ of the brigade or, rather, the assistant commander for security. And we've already discussed professional management.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the small squares at the bottom are security organs in the battalions within the composition of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the rectangle and squares itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday on page 23392 of the transcript -- thank you, we are finished with that document. It can be removed from our screens. Anyway, lines 17 to 23 in response to a question from my learned friend, Mr. McCloskey, you explained the duties of the company military police commander to follow the commander within the frame works of the orders given. Now, my question to you is this: The security organ, can it issue instructions to the commander of a military police company outside the frameworks of a commander's orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mrs. Nikolic, a security organ does not have the competence and authority to issue any instructions which are outside the orders issued by the commander because that would mean an expansion of his own authority, which he does not have the right to, nor does he have authorisation to do any things like that. So no, he cannot issue such instructions. Let me just add, it is understood that when this -- we are talking about the implementation of the orders issued by the commander of the military police. We have to very precise there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: However, if this order or instruction would be contrary to the law, would the commander of the military police company be duty-bound to act on it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Nobody has the right to implement any unlawful instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we now have the break so that I can re-organize my questions and finish as quickly as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had discussed the issue with my colleagues during the break, and we've reached an agreement, and it's really a question of principal. So as to the issues of water supply, my colleague will raise those issues quite independently since it's a general question. However, with regard to P2517, that document directly and exclusively pertains to my client; hence -- while my client has chosen me as his lawyer, so I think it really behooves me to ask the questions if you will allow this. I don't think that someone else can do this in my stead. Indeed, I'm convinced that it's a question of principle. It's not the case in this particular case, but it's possible that there could be a conflict of interest, and it may not always be possible for one defence counsel to ask questions in the place of another Defence counsel. I think we have to abide by very specific rules when the Prosecutor raises a completely new question during the cross-examination. The witness has been here for a week. The name of my client was never mentioned during the interrogation in chief, nor by the counsel of Popovic or Nikolic. No document mentioning my client was mentioned or submitted. So for the he very first time, my client's name was mentioned by the trial attorney. Hence, I think that based on the fundamental rights of the accused I should be entitled to ask questions regarding this specific document. I will not mention the water tower. That is a general question that is of interest to all of the Defence counsels and, therefore, questions may be raised by any of them. I believe that it is a fundamental right of the accused as any accused has the right to be judged in joint trial as if he were the only accused, and if he were the only accused, of course, this question would not arise. If we allow the Prosecution to use new documents, and when I say new, it's new with this witness. Of course, the document was submitted to other witnesses, but I don't see why I should have been expected to raise this with the witness when the issue had not been mentioned. So if we allow the Prosecutor in the cross-examination to raise a new question and do not allow the Defence counsel to ask questions on that same issue, the Defence would then not enjoy the same rights as a Prosecution, and an accused in a joint trial would not enjoy the same rights as if he were being tried alone. So I would ask you for the right to ask questions only on the document P2517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Madam Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, having had a little time to think about this, my mentioning of General Miletic was only in reading who the document was to and kind of going over the date, referring who it was to, and at one point I remember emphasizing that this was a proposal and not an order because I think the witness or the translation started talking about order. But I never did anything to try to implicate General Miletic in anything except just to read the document about it, which -- a document that has been around for a long time. So had I done something to specifically - for lack of a better word - ding General Miletic, I think she would have an argument. In this case, I don't think she does. However, if she goes into this with this witness in an area that I did not go into, she will be opening the door to an area that the Prosecution may then want to get into. Having said all that, if she wants to make an exploratory question on this issue, on whether General Miletic is authorised to give orders, perhaps it will be over and done with in a question or two. But I think we can see the slippery slope where this takes us, and that's why I've objected thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of words, Your Honour. We second Mrs. Faveau's position because it is a principle that we want to abide by. If that principle and that right is curtailed, we wouldn't be in the position to examine our witnesses in a proper manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think the principle has already been discussed and disposed of weeks ago, so we are -- we won't be opening that chapter again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Faveau, we would like to know the precise questions that you wish to put to the witness before we decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are only two questions, in fact, the first being whether General Mladic [Realtime transcript read in error "Miletic"] was the only person who had the authority to approve or endorse such proposals within the staff of the Army Republika Srpska; and the second question is according to the information that the witness has, does he have any information that would suggest that those proposals were followed or implemented or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My memory of the witness's answers, it was -- he was trying to distance himself from this document and the subjects that I was dealing with, the chemical weapons and the bombing refugees. And so to ask him now a question, you know, a leading question about General Mladic in this context I think is objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, there's a mistake in the transcript, I said General Mladic, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, that correction needs to be made to line 18 of the previous page, page 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision is to allow only the first question but not the second, Ms. Faveau. And the reasons should be obvious, particularly since the letter was addressed to your client, although neither the witness nor the Prosecution has tried to implicate your client. Yes, we need the witness in the courtroom now, please. Ms. Nikolic will conclude her -- Ms. Nikolic will finish, will conclude her -- Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I complete my redirect and then have Ms. Faveau putting questions? What would be your decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's precisely what we were discussing. We seem to be in agreement once you've started your redirect, and you are halfway through, that you conclude it first. After all, you know what the question is going to be, although we don't know what the answer is likely to be. So let's proceed with your redirect, and then we'll give the opportunity to Ms. Faveau. The idea is not to interrupt your redirect any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to continue with my questions. By referring to your testimony on the 4th of July, 2008, it is page 23344 of the transcript. You were asked a number of questions concerning the general staff of the VRS instruction P2741. Among other questions, you were also asked by my learned friend what the problems and irregularities appeared in the command and control chain of the OB referred to in the instruction and which caused instruction to be draft. Your reply was that you did not study the process of drafting instructions and their causes. However, I still have a question for you. In principle, can one deem opening mail packages or assigning a security organ to duty shifts or refusing to allow vehicles to be used or to take away the stamp used by the security organ; can these be deemed irregularities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic, as far as I recall in terms of my answers, it was not in strict accordance with what I said. This may have happened because of the interpretation. I said that I had prior experience with the JNA but that I did not study this in particular when drafting this report. However, it is not directly relevant to your question. I just wanted to have that down for the record. First and foremost, the instruction and its drafting was caused because -- by certain problems that had been identified in the VRS during the preceding period up to the instruction itself. The problems are outlined in the instruction according to their consequences and the situation that was established in the field. The instruction envisages how the problems should be dealt with in terms of command and control. It has to do with command and control. It is limited to the application of the rules of service because it talks about the tasks of security organs as prescribed by the rules of service of security organs. Anything beyond the rules in terms of deviating from point 93 of the rules of service and point 48 of the same rules was seen as an infraction of command and control that had been prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I mentioned several examples in my question of such irregularities or infractions. Are these, indeed, infractions of the rules of service of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: That's why I mentioned point 93 of the rules of service as well as 48, which stipulates that the competent officer can issue tasks to the security organ within the security organ's remit, which are not done regularly in terms of establishment, but, however, are still part of the scope of activities of the security organ. Item 93 states that security organs are not appointed to perform duty shifts in internal services. According to the rules of work of commands and staffs at page 34 and 35, what we have are the organs of internal services including operational duty services and others to which security organs were assigned according to the documentation I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will move on to item 2 of the instruction. It is transcript page 23345 and 23346. In e-court, I would kindly ask for P2741 to be brought up. While we are waiting for the instruction, Colonel -- well, so as not to waste any time, I wanted to read out the text of item 2. You've already testified about it. It is the third paragraph in B/C/S as well as in English in item 2: "All members of these organs in the service have the legal authority and act upon those in the course of their work in keeping with the instruction provided by the state security service." You've explained all that. In your report, which is 3D396, did you deal with a full explanation of all five areas of competence assigned to the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: In my report, you can see the authorities of security organs, the five of them, which are also assigned to the state security service and its internal organs or organs of the interior. In keeping with the rules of work of the security organ, security organs cannot be prevented from using these authorities provided they abide by law.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: 3D396, page 14, 15 of the B/C/S and 16 and 17 of the English version: That is your report, Mr. Vuga. In particular, 282 and 287, those are the points I'm interested in. 3D396, 14 and 15 in the B/C/S and 16 and 17 in the English. Page 14 of the B/C/S, please. We have it on our screens, but is that the portion of your report which deals in detail with OB authorisations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is the part of my report dealing with those questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't need the document anymore. Now, on transcript page 23347 of the 4th of July, 2008, when referring to the same document P2741, you testified about providing intelligence information or, rather, in point 4 of the instructions. So once again, P2741 on our screens, please, in e-court. Page 2 in the B/C/S. While we are waiting for the document to appear, I have a general question for you. Tell us, please, Colonel, what happened on the 13th of January in the Army of Republika Srpska - that is the 13th of January, 1995, of course - along the lines of the questions asked to you by Mr. Haynes and linked to security and intelligence affairs within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mrs. Nikolic, on the 13th of January, 1995, an order from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska led to differentiation in functions, security and intelligence organs to intelligence organs, which were incorporated within the composition of the staff itself, and the functions of the security organ separately, which remained within the frameworks of the commands under the command of the commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you testified about that, you may differentiated between intelligence and security information. Now, my question to you is this: After this January 1995, in the brigade, who were -- was intelligence information sent to, and to whom was security information sent to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: In the brigade from the moment these functions were separated and from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, but are we talking brigades generally or a particular brigade, a motorised brigade, a light infantry brigade? This makes a big difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, which brigade are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that's clear enough now. Colonel, perhaps you can answer the question directing your answer to the Zvornik Brigade, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have understood that. The answer for the Zvornik Brigade is this: That the intelligence organ, which was within the composition of the security intelligence organ of the brigade, was transferred and dislocated from establishment, was to become part of the staff of the brigade, and it was the intelligence organ within the staff of the brigade. The security organ remained subordinated directly to the commander, and intelligence went to the staff of the brigade to the intelligence organ there and the Chief of Staff, of course, as his superior officer. Security information went to the -- down the professional line of the security organ and were in the security organ for use and evaluation and everything else that the security organs had under their authority and accessible to the commander pursuant to regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before point 4, it says simultaneously the members of the intelligence and security organs, they weren't separated yet, are duty-bound to inform their immediate commanders about their assessments and et cetera in the extent to which it refers to the security of the units and institutions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise to the interpreters for going so fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: -- in the assessments and observations, a necessary scope and measure, which relate to security of the unit -- of the units and institutions, and that is on page 2 of P2274, the first paragraph in the B/C/S and on page 2 of the English. Colonel, is that what you were talking about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mrs. Nikolic, this is part of what I was talking about earlier on, the part relating to the functions of the security organ as realized in the command within whose composition the security organs find themselves; and it is their basic responsibility, that is to say to protect the security of their unit and command, the ones that they are responsible to the commander -- responsible for to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go on to point 5 of that same document. It is page 23348 of the transcript, once again of the 4th of July, 2008. You testified about promotions and replacements in the OB, and my question to you is as follows: If a commander learns that his security organ has committed a crime of any sort or has violated the law, does the commander have the right to take steps and proceedings against the security organ with the aim of replacing him -- having him replaced?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mrs. Nikolic, the security organs did not have any immunity, did not enjoy immunity when it came to responsibility for crimes committed or any other type of responsibility which was prescribed in the rules and regulations of the Army Republika Srpska, the Criminal Code, and other regulations and provisions providing for sanctions for controversion of the law, infractions of the law. The commander could initiate proceedings just as he could against any perpetrator of a crime or somebody to be held accountable for their conduct under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now, in keeping with item 5 - may we see item 5, please - in the sense of stimulative measures and proposals of the security organs, who makes assessments of the work of the security organs? Who assesses their work?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mrs. Nikolic, an assessment and appraisal of the work of the security organs is something made by the commander, and in that regard he needs to be informed about a significant portion of the work of the security organs in the field of counterintelligence, which as a rule are not given insight to -- to people at all levels. So that is necessary for an evaluation to be realistic and all-embracing. Otherwise, it would be partial with all the drawbacks that such a partial appraisal involves.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to point 7 of this document now, which is on page 3 of the B/C/S. It is the control of professionalism and legality of the OB, Document 25741, and you testified about that on page 23351 of the transcript in response to Mr. Haynes's questions. My question to you is this: If the security organ violates any regulations in going about its duties and performing its tasks of the duty operative in the brigade or in conducting affairs with the military police, who controls the professionality and legality of the work of security organs in these affairs according to item 7 of the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mrs. Nikolic, I'd like to ask you to clarify what you mean. I'm not sure I understood your question. It was incomplete, I feel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that. If a security organ, for instance, violates a regulation or is in contravention of the law in performing its counterintelligence work in the Judas Operation, for example, who controls and supervises the legality of its work within the framework of that area of its activity?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I see what you are asking me now, yes. Professional supervision and legality in work in full when it comes to the methods of work applied by the security organs, that is done exclusively by the superior security organ within the frameworks of the line of professional management and supervision, down that chain, right down to the level of the individual who is authorised or who decides about the use of and selection of methods of work. The person who approved the application of those methods of work, that same person has the right fully to control the legality of their implementation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In a case where the security organ is engaged in affairs of a duty officer, for example, or has dealings with the military police, who then controls its professionalism and the legality of its work?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Professionality and legality of work for the security organs engaged in the areas you mentioned in your question is controlled by the unit commander or, rather, the senior officer who prescribed those duties within the unit and who is in command of the unit within that sphere of activity. And we once again come back to the commander of the unit and the security organ as a member of the command and assistant to the command of full security is responsible for those affairs to the commander fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the next document on e-court, P176. And the document was shown to you during your testimony on Friday, pages 23354 and 23355 of the transcript. Let me remind you, it is a warning to keep confidential information confidential, P176, secret information secret.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please clarify the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P, Prosecution, 176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are being told it's not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. It was already used on Friday, I believe, but my associate tells me it is 7D P00176 is the number, and it's an exhibit under that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it an order from the security department, 3rd of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is an issue of warning, a caution. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's Prosecution Exhibit 176. Looking at the number, it should be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, this is a document of the 5th corps, the security department, on the protection of the leaking of secret information. It was sent to the commander, the 503rd motorised brigade, that is to say the Zvornik Brigade, and it was signed by Momcilo Pajic, an officer of the Drina Corps. My question to you is this: The information and data that are protected in communication in counterintelligence work done by the OB, are they protected in fact by any rules and regulations of the OB service governing the OB, the rules of service to which this document refers, security rules of service and its provisions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. We've gone through this, and they are, and I don't know why we are going through it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This question was broached in a different way during the cross-examination conducted by my learned friend Mr. Haynes, so I'd like us to complete the document in the manner that it deserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd also like to say it's a leading question, but -- are the rules of the OB which are referred to in this document, it just invites the answer "yes," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe there's something coming, but we don't see it yet, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, please rephrase your question and make sure that in doing so you do not repeat or elicit the repetition of information that has already been given by the witness during the

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will follow your instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, in this document - I will read out a portion of it - it says: "In the future, all mail addressed to the OB should not be opened. The counterintelligence organ is responsible to its department. It should also familiarize the commander with the important elements. The security organ based on its rights and obligations, which stem from the rules of service and the applicable law, have the right to use the unit's seal. Given that you are familiar with the contents of the documents of this department, and I won't go into all the numbers, you are duty-bound to provide a written statement to the security organ of your unit on the keeping of secret information, Article 25, paragraph 2, of the rules of security or safety." Could we next have P470 in e-court, page 10 in the B/C/S and 11 and 12 in the English. After that, I will put my question. P470, page 10 in the B/C/S and 11 and 12 in the English version. 470.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. 407.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [In English] 407, please. [Interpretation] Page 10 in the B/C/S, 11 and 12 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could we please move the document so as to be able to see the right-hand side of the B/C/S version. Colonel, please have a look at the document before you. Item 25. Does this rule, number 25 that the document refers to - that is P4176; that is the letter sent to the commander of the 503rd Brigade - does it refer to that rule?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, that is the rule referred to in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Item 2 of Rule 25 says, "The officers managing security organs and other persons who get by -- information which falls under the scope of activity of the OB by whichever means have to keep such data according to the rules in place under protection of secrecy." Also in paragraph 4 it says, "the obligation to protect information" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Persons under paragraph 3 of this item shall give a special written statement concerning the obligation to protect the secrecy of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Colonel, according to this rule are all persons, should they get by certain information, are obliged to keep them secret and provide written statements about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: All persons are duty-bound to treat the data which has to do with methods of work of the security organ and information gained by their application if arrived at by whichever means have to keep them as secret under different categories of classification up to the level of state secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does that mean, Colonel, that that category of persons includes commanders and all those who get in contact with secret information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: All persons without exception, irrespective of their function, position, and other attributes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we again have P176. It is the OB letter that we just saw. Thank you. I will read item 6 in which it says, "We hope that you shall see this as an effort in good faith to protect the security service." Could this be seen as a disciplinary measure or warning which may carry consequences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Colonel. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This is leading, and it's all clearly an argument that's being made through this witness. It's not appropriate redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I join that objection. This is not the proper examination of a witness. Two sections of two documents have been read out to him at length, and the link is just being made through him. It doesn't need any expertise. This is a closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's hear your new question. Mr. Haynes in particular has made a point, and it goes across to some of the previous questions that you have put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear your question as rephrased, Ms. Nikolic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: My question, Colonel, is this: Does the document before you in your professional expert opinion, is it a document which initiates a disciplinary proceedings or procedure by the OB against anyone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. Don't answer the question. Of course, the document says what it reads, so let's continue with your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On the 4th of July at page 23340, you testified about a document from 1992. Could we please have Document 7D483 brought up in e-court. 7D483. This document was issued by the 17th Corps command, which was a unit of the former JNA, on the 25th of February, 1992, sent personally to the commanders of subordinate units. Colonel, please tell us what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: This is an order/warning on the engagement of security organs in units. The document warns that the rules of engagement of the OB in the various units should be strictly abided by. We have commented upon it rather extensively in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was this document sent to any of the security organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: This is a corps command document which followed the chain of command and had to do with unit commanders rather than security organs directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something about a document which was also shown to you on Friday. It is Exhibit P3033; pages of the transcript are 2334 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 23354.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It has to do with the Judas operational action. P3033. Thank you. My question is this: According to this document, if the senior officers, Mladic and Tolimir or Mladic or Tolimir, are to arrive to the brigade, is the commander supposed to know about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: As regards these officers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- one moment. I remember quite vividly this question being asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have only two additional questions concerning the measures undertaken in such cases, and that is something that remains unclear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then go straight to that, ma'am, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In such a case, Mr. Vuga, are any security measures put in place at the command, and do such measures have anything to do with the counterintelligence work of the security organ undertaken concerning the planned murder which was to be part of the operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: All security measures undertaken comprise a single security system. The counterintelligence measures are only undertaken by the security organ. Their nature is as prescribed by the regulation. I won't go into that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If these highly ranked people are to arrive at the unit, who is responsible for their security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mrs. Nikolic, although imprecise -- although your question was imprecise, my answer would be this: Those security system elements that are in place are supposed to be responsible in their respective domains. It is precisely described what the responsibility was of certain security elements, are, per functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If we go beyond this document, apart from the counterintelligence work of the Judas Operation, who was responsible for the security of these officers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I believe my previous answer contains the part that has to do with the system elements. The different security system elements range from the duty officer and the soldier at the gate up to the commander of security if he is there. These are all different parts of the system. Each of them has its tasks and responsibilities for their implementation. Counterintelligence work is a part of that system, and the way they should be undertaken are -- is described in the regulations. However, it is not to be disclosed to those who are not supposed to take part in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just -- I think it's a translation error. Commander of security?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Lines 3 and 4. He is referring to lines 3 and 4 on this page, page 46. I don't know. I can't answer your question because, obviously, I don't understand the B/C/S language, so I don't know what the witness said. We can ask him. Colonel, you said the different security system elements range from the duty officer and a soldier at the gate up to the -- did you say the commander of security if he is there, or did you use any other different term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commander of the unit, not security. The unit and its commander prescribe the security regimen within its competence. These are the parts of the system I referred to, which need to function jointly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, I have one more question.
