Today on page 15 of the transcript, lines 8 to 13, and my colleague was asking you a question, my learned friend Mr. McCloskey, and the question was, if the main commander in any army decide to kill many hundreds of prisoners in an operation, which implies incarceration, transport, execution, burial, and everything else, not to have to repeat the whole question. Anyway, he ended by saying that is it -- does it go about saying that it should be an action conducted speedily, quietly, and so on as the question was worded. My colleague then went on to ask you, which military service would be the best to use for the security of such an operation, would be the military service of choice? Now, your answer was as follows, and my question to you is, according to the documents which you looked through and everything else, the operation of incarcerating prisoners of war, which occurred in Bratunac and Zvornik, was it done according to the so-called secret plan, speedily, efficiently, and quietly; or did you -- or what was your position in the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is commenting on his opinion about the specific acts in the case, which he has not yet given his opinion on as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, do you agree with Mr. McCloskey? In other words, are you in a position to give us an answer to Ms. Nikolic's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all I can say is what I found in the documents and how I understood this and recognised it in the light of the activities that were undertaken according to a plan which would have the kind of character that we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what would your answer be in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the activities and documents that I analysed, there are a series of facts which do not satisfy the criteria of a secret plan or even a plan, per se, in general terms. And they are as follows. Well, some of them because there are more which are a little less important, but bear out what I'm saying. First of all, activities which would move along the lines of liquidation of the prisoners of war or their execution, whichever term you like to use, would have in front of them much that would not be publicly demonstrated or visible to a large number of observers, for example, participants and those who would be supposed to keep it secret. So that is the portion that is lacking. First of all, incarceration in Bratunac itself, imprisonment as a stage which in case a plan existed must certainly have been avoided; secondly, moving the people from Bratunac to other locations to inhabited areas, into an environment during the day would almost be publicly demonstrated, which, if you need to have secrecy, this must be avoided; doing this in that way must be avoided; thirdly, documents that speak to the offer that prisoners of war should be transported to the economia for work and sent that way, so that offer by the officers and in positions such as General Tolimir occupied would not exist if a plan had existed to keep this action secret. The execution of prisoners of war in places where this was done in relation to the facilities to which they were deployed speaks about a lack of covering up this fact, and I have to use a very logical observation here. Even those who in a way learned of this or were they to learn of it would have asked the question, now, if they wanted to kill them, why wouldn't they have taken them to a more secretive place and killed them there and not here, so all that led me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop because you've now moved from the documents to areas where you are just trying to make one and one and together without really knowing what happened and what didn't. And one question from me. In such a case if such a plan existed, how much documentation or documents would you expect to find in any case if it's the kind of plan that was suggested to you and the kind of secrecy that would have been necessary? How much documentation would you have expected to find?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I made the observations I did from the existing documents as much as was contained in them except for the last thing I said, that is to say the synthesis, and I can correct that. However, I had not expected to find -- I did not expect to finds the document of a secret plan, but did I expect that in the procedures and steps I would have recognised something that would have belonged and been commensurate with a secret plan. So that was the substance -- that's the substance of what I'm saying. So I did my best in the procedure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Faveau, your two question -- your one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I have one question for you, and to this end I'd like to call up Document P2517. While it is being displayed, let me tell you that this is the document that General Tolimir sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on the July 20th, 1995, document where he was using about the -- where he was talking about the use of chemical weapons. This is Document 2517. In this document, notably in paragraphs 5 and 6, there are -- these seem to be proposals that General Tolimir would have sent to the Main Staff. I would like to know the following: Do you agree that in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska the only person that had the authority to approve such proposals was General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: In the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, it was only General Mladic as far as the Main Staff was concerned and activities within it who was responsible and had the authority to approve or refute proposals by his subordinates and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Faveau. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given that new area that's just been opened, I would like to ask him a question about that topic. One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why, then, would he make this specifically to the attention of General Miletic in his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yeah, but you could have asked that question to him when you were -- but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I wasn't trying to mess with General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll take the question ourselves to try to keep it as short as possible. Colonel, why would Tolimir write to Miletic, write this letter or -- to Miletic and not to Mladic directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Information and proposals which were supposed to be formed could be collected in one place or should be collected in one place before they reach General Mladic because otherwise he would be inundated with proposals arriving to him, coming into him directly. Not this one but others. He had his organs who would amass those proposals and then present them to him. That is how things worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Re-examination by Zivanovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vuga. Good afternoon. During my examination, I'd like to clarify some of the things that the Prosecutor asked you about, so let's take a look first at a document that was shown to you yesterday, 1D1078. Let's just wait for the English translation. Yesterday, you spoke in detail while you addressed the last page of the document that was shown to you yesterday. I'd now like to draw your attention to the first page of this document. On the first page, can you see to whom this report was addressed? Who was it sent to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, what I can see is that the report was sent to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me this: When a document is sent to the command of a unit in general, to whom is it actually being sent? Who opens the document? Who takes up the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: A document headed in this way would go to the commander of the unit because no other organ is stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the witness see the last page to address this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that context, can you take a look at the second page of this document, and it was shown to you yesterday, and look at the last three points where it says that it was sent to the chief of security, the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, and the archive. Can you now explain to me whether that means that in addition to the document being sent to the commander it is also sent to these three instances, or was it just sent to the three people mentioned at the bottom of the document or places?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: This was -- would have been sent -- this "sent to" would be in slight contradiction to the title, the heading, but I have to mention in that regard the following: The chief of security was the person who was responsible to the commander as far as the military police was concerned, so on that basis the title itself and what it says here are not contradictory. So whether it went to the chief of security or whether the document as it said at the top of the document went to the commander, it must have reached the commander. That's the conclusion I can make, but I don't know the fate of this document because I have no trace of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The top of the page doesn't say "commander." It says "command."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When -- Your Honour, when the command receives documents, where it says "to the command" without the actual person within the command stipulated to whom the document should go, then it would have to be given to the commander because no other organ is designated. And at the bottom, it says to the chief of the staff, so it would go to him, but I was talking about the heading, the title. And then it also says to whom it was sent, so the title says to the commander, and the distribution was done in this way, but I have no trace as to how it was actually done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you go further, if you could remind me to which organ this 5th military police battalion belongs. It is organ of Drina Corps or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the 5th Battalion of the military police was a unit at the command of the Drina Corps or, rather, subordinated to the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The Prosecutor yesterday asked you something about the use of force and permission given by the minister, and he said that he found that in your report. Now, could you tell me in very definite terms if you remember whether you used anywhere that expression that the minister or, rather, that sentence that the minister approves the use of force or allows for the use of force in your report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, this may be a translation issue, but the term that I was quoting from was "coercion," and that was what was in the report in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that was what we had in the transcript except in one instance when it was interpreted as "correction" instead of "coerced," but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. In your report, does it say anywhere that the minister approves the use of force or coercion or any other act resembling that, so was the minister mentioned in your report as somebody who can approve something like that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: In my work and in my report and investigations, that question was not a point of consideration, a question to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But that was an express question put to you by the Prosecutor on page 23378, lines 13 to 15 of the transcript. Now, the next thing that I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Maybe we have a translation issue here, but I quoted him from his report this term, and it was on the screen. Everybody saw it. The Colonel saw it, and if this is going to be asked again, I can read it back, but -- it's 1D1175, paragraph 2.13: "Authorised military personnel in the military security service and military police may use while performing military security or military police duties weapons and other means of coercion under conditions prescribed for authorised officials of the interior." And I think I asked about the minister of interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Minister was not mentioned but the law, law authorizing the members of security to use arm and coercion in some situations, and it was a part of testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says "officials of the interior," and so if the question is going to be asked, it should include the proper part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it is to the officials of the -- to the officials of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, your question was going to be as rephrased as follows: In your report does it say anywhere that the minister - you can add now or other officer - approves the use of force, coercion, or any other act resembling that. So was the minister or such other officer mentioned in your report as somebody who could approve something like that? I mean, I have read it as it is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Once again, let me rephrase the question. In your report, does it say that a person outside the situations prescribed by war can approve the use of force or coercion or something similar to a member of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, outside the regulations and situations in which those authorisations are applied, nobody can expand them to include anything else except for what has already been stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: From your report, one would say that the use of force is regulated by the law, clearly stating -- and coercion clearly stating what cannot and cannot -- can and cannot be done. Is this something unique to Serbia or the RS, or have such solutions been come up with in other countries as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: All security systems that I know of - that is, beyond Serbia and the RS - have the authority to counter dangerous activities and use force within certain limits, i.e., coercion, the use of force and coercion. Well, I'm not familiar with the English language, and I can't say what theic exact difference is, but I would stick with coercion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If I understood you well, under the regulation -- well, first of all, could you tell us who puts the conditions in place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: They are made part of Article 151 of the Law On Criminal Procedure. There we find what the authority is of the persons who are authorised to apply such procedures as stipulated in the rules of service for the security organ and in the rules of service of the military police for the military police. Those situations are clearly defined. They are there to do away with any risk or danger which was identified and required attention and intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us clarify some methodological elements that you included in your report. You were asked about it by the Prosecutor at page 23383 yesterday. Would your report be of any value if you based it, say, on an accused's statement, if the accused would share with you something that he recalls or wants you to know? Would that be a good quality expert report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: When researching such topics as this one, in order to arrive at reliable conclusions and facts used to arrive at that conclusion and to also make those facts as watertight as possible, then testimonies and witness statements must be severely restricted or even avoided for the risk that that would entail. That could bring into question the validity of conclusions reached if one used witness statements. I did not use witness statements because I did not come across sufficiently reliable facts and information which would be beyond any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, non-responsive. The question was related to accused statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't know what your answer would be, but I will try to put the question again. When we are talking about an accused's statement, would that be a solid basis for a quality expert work in this field, the information that you would receive in that way?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: For me as an expert, an accused's statement is on the level of the witness statement. I have no reason to single an accused out of, say, any other witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As a professional, would you accept to draft an expert report which would be based on the information served to you by me serving my interests as Defence counsel and that I would require you to use that in drafting your report? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: This is not my first report. The principal question of all expert analyses is whether they satisfy the threshold or the standards of profession, and they should not be drafted based on anyone's requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have a break. We had a break earlier, previous break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you think you need to finish your redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I hope to the end of the business day today, until the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right? I mean, I don't think it's fair to keep this gentleman here any further. We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zivanovic, I'm informed the witness is quite tired, so please try to -- I'm not going to keep him again and get him to return tomorrow. We need to finish with him today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he is able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he is able, but we need to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, in answer to a question from the Prosecutor yesterday on page 23393 and 94, you spoke about the actions in the surrounding villages in which individual civilians participated too. Now, I'd like to ask you whether from the documents that you had an opportunity of seeing were able to see whether any difference could be established between civilians and the BH Army, members of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. I think this is more time-consuming than probative, especially since his answer to my questions on that topic were not responsive to my question, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. Let's move on, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is there any possibility at all for you as an expert or, rather, can you tell us whether the Army of Republika Srpska could make a difference between the civilians who were attacking, taking part in attacks on villages, and those who were not doing that, who were dealing with farming and so on as Mr. McCloskey said, farmers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, please, Colonel. Move to your next question, Mr. Zivanovic, your next topic, actually, not your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey showed you a document of the 19th of November, 1992, which speaks about the treatment among others of the population, the inhabitants, the Muslim inhabitants, Muslim population. Now, would you take a look at another document, now, please, and then explain to us something about that. It is 1D1302. This is a report --

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I just have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, that document hasn't been translated into B/C/S. It is a report by the -- by Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki of the United Nations of February the -- or rather, the 23rd or February, 1993, special rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights. Let's move to page 18 of that document, please. I'd like us to look at paragraph 88. I'm going to read it out to you, just one sentence. It says, "Violations of the Geneva Conventions [In English] were perpetrated by government forces when they refused to allow the ever creation of the civilian population from Srebrenica, thus attempting to use them as a human shield."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't object as long as he will read the preceding paragraph, 87. There is a B/C/S translation under 3312.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I should tender all document into evidence and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but you are asking a question now. We are not expecting the witness to read the entire document. Mr. McCloskey is telling you that he would not object to the question if it is -- paragraph 87 is also read out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 87, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. "Massive and repeated violation of Geneva Conventions of 1949 were perpetrated in a recent combat in Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were carried out by Serb forces in Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica in attacking and ambushing civilians attempting to flee their encirclement in attacking the villages themselves. In refusing to allow humanitarian aid to enter and refusing to allow the ever creation of the wounded in attempt to link the above issues to the independent question of freedom of movement for Serbs in Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now my question is this: Can you explain to us in the first paragraph that I read out, that is to say 88, what does "human shield" mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Human shield is a concept that has been known for far longer than what is stated here. They are civilian persons who are protected according to international conventions and covenants and according to which no -- and they are not to be attacked, and they are placed in front of military units, and in that way what is intended is to paralyze the effects of the opposing side and reduce the possibility of them firing at units behind the human shield or within a mixed population. So those persons who are protected protect those who are not subject to protection and protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, within this context, let's look at 1D628, please. 1D628. [In English] Not 3628 but 628.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Document 1D628 is not available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy of it in front of you, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. The document is -- 628 is available in e-court. 1D. 1D.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Try 5D496, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have it in e-court under 1D628.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it this one? All right. Then let's proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't think this document has been translated, but in any case, it is just one sentence that I want to address. Oh, yes. It is translated. Good. Just briefly, can you tell us who sent this document and to whom it was sent?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The document was sent from the command of the 2nd corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, take a look at point 5 of this document, paragraph 5. Tell me, please, do you understand this, this sentence, "Under no circumstances is a single inhabitant ought to move away from the demilitarised zone." Can you tell me whether this point can be understood as being an order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Item 5 is an express order because it says "under no circumstances".

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the date of this document, now, up at the top. Can you see the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The date is the 5th of July, 1993, Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask you to look at a document together with me, which I have here on paper. I don't think you have it. It is a document that was shown to you by my learned friend of the Prosecution, and it is about the water tower. So can we take a look now at Document 3501. If it's too much of an effort for you to read it, I can read it out to you because I know you have some sight problems, and you can just follow. Would that be easier?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, it would be easier if you read it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So this is a document dated the 21st of June 1993. It was sent to the commander of the Drina Corps in person, and it is signed by the commander Colonel Vukota Vukotic. The text of this document read as follows: On the 26th of May at 2058 hours, the Turks launched a surprise violent infantry attack on the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska along the stretch of road and river of Zeleni Jadar at a stretch of about 2 and a half kilometres. The focus of the attack was along the road and river of Zeleni Jadar. The attack lasted for 2 hours and 40 minutes. The RS army soldiers returned fire from all available weapons, and the Turks' attack was completely repelled except for sporadic shooting. The fire stopped at around 2400 hours. Considering that it was a dark night and foggy with occasional rain and wind, the Turks succeeded in infiltrating 2 DTG - that is to say, as far as I know the abbreviation for sabotage and terrorist group - along the Zeleni Jadar river. The first sabotage terrorist group sabotaged the water work pipes in the vicinity of the Sipa factory at some 150 metres away from the UNPROFOR observation checkpoint. We do not know the number of terrorists, and something has been crossed out there. I can't read what it says. The other group of terrorists succeeded to come to the water. The explosion at the pipes in the factory was of medium strength, and it was deafening from the water filters. Hearing the explosion from the Zeleni Jadar valley, the commanding officers realized that a diversion had taken place at the water works facility and that that was actually the main target of the Turks' surprise and very fierce attack and that everything else was just camouflage so that the saboteurs could go sabotaging without any disturbances. Judging by the traces left when the terrorists pulled out after the destruction of the water tower and water filters and that this destruction was done by a strong explosive and - could we zoom down the document, please, in English, thank you - and we can't see any traces on the basis of which we could assess the character nature of the explosives and the explosive devices. On the 27th of May, the next day, when they met with UNPROFOR, when I met with UNPROFOR, I lodged a complaint with the major from Canada and said that the previous night they served as a protection to the Muslim terrorists to be able to destroy facilities unimpeded so that they could accuse us before the world of the so-called vandalism just as they always did, we couldn't have directed the focus of fire towards the stretch checkpoint Zeleni Jadar because we didn't want to endanger the UNPROFOR forces, which were located at the observation point and which they saw for themselves. They replied in the affirmative to my claims but disgusted by the Muslim's behaviour. During the following two meetings with UNPROFOR, in the context of criticizing the Muslims for not implementing the obligations under taken under the agreement on the surrender of weapons, I reiterated and emphasized that they were so cunning and so evil that they were committing the most horrible sabotage actions on structures and let alone what they would do to us Serbs. I don't think I have to read on. I don't need to read the last paragraph, but I wanted to ask you something. Is there anything in this text of the telegram whether the details indicate that all this was pure fabrication and untruthful? In a word, can this information be checked out? It is very viable?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: As far as the text is concerned and an analysis which I conduct when I'm confronted with a text and have to analyse a text, it is only by a parallel method of comparison, comparing it -- the events with the text and with the consequences if they are accessible to me in a document. Only on that basis am I able to ascertain whether there are certain lackings and shortcomings between the facts which are to be found in either three of these things. I don't have the possibility of doing that here, so I can say that within the frameworks of this text -- I can just make my assessments on the basis of the text itself. There are no such factors if this text were to be considered sufficient for it to be interpreted on its own.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's now go back to a document that the Prosecutor showed you yesterday, and I'm sure you will remember that in this document we are dealing with the 26th of May, whereas on the 27th of May a protest was lodged with UNPROFOR. Now, I'd like us to go back to the document, as I was saying, that the Prosecutor showed you. It is 3499, the number. Can you tell us what the date of this document is? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Well, if I can see it properly, I'll read it out and you can correct me if I'm wrong. It says the 31st of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us after -- or, rather, how many days that is from the event described in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Judging by the date and the previous date, which was the 26th, the difference is five days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you read this document, does it follow from what it says here that the water tower at that point in time had not been demolished and as far as we can read from this document that this should be done the following day, on the 1st of June, if this document is to be believed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: The chronology of events denies the contents if you compare the state of the water tower on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to take you back for a moment to paragraph 3. Perhaps I read it too fast, so perhaps you weren't able to understand it properly. Judging by the traces and where the terrorists pulled out from after the water tower event and the water filters, there were five of them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How do you understand this: Water tower, then it says mistake, water filter.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I understand it as saying that it wasn't the water tower that was destroyed, but that the water filter was damaged so that the system itself couldn't function properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And now let me ask you something else now because we have some information about this. Do you know whether at that time - and we are talking about 1992, the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 - whether the water works in Bratunac was functioning properly, if you happen to know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: I can't answer that question with any certitude because I don't actually have the information or knowledge to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I want to ask you just this, another thing: Yesterday, my learned friend of the Prosecution asked you about some derogatory terms that were used for -- when referring to Muslims, and among others he showed you some documents where the term "balija" is mentioned. And he asked you whether there is a term that is worse from the term "balija." Now, as a security professional, can you differentiate and make grades between insulting words, say which are more insulting than others? Is that something that you can do as being the professional you are in your field?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I've already answered that question. I answered it yesterday, and so I'll have to repeat that today. And it is this: I do not know all the aspects and contents of the concept of "balija," the term "balija," because I didn't live in an environment where that term was used. Now, as far as the different grades of derogatory meaning and everything else, that does not come within the field of my expertise, nor did I attempt in any way at all to interpret it in drawing conclusions. So my answer is no, that is not my profession, and I can't give an answer which would be deemed satisfactory to a question like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else now. In analyzing these documents, I'm sure you looked at documents where the members of the Army Republika Srpska were referred to as Chetniks. Do you remember something like that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, when reading a document like that, can you assess the context in which this term Chetnik was used, for instance? What does it denote? Is it a favourable term, a neutral term, a derogatory term? How do you understand the use of this word "Chetnik" in the documents you came across?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need an expert like Colonel Vuga to answer that question? Haven't we heard enough about Ustasha, Chetnik, balija? Let's move to your next topic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you one more question. I think that will suffice. Would you look at your report, now, 1175. 1D1175 is the number, and it is page 20 of the English and 18 of the B/C/S. Let's take a look at the following paragraphs. Paragraph 2 -- let me just check that out. 2.1 -- 16, I think. Just let me take a moment. No, I'm sorry. Can we take a look at pages 7 and 10. I do apologise. 7 and 10, please, 7 being the English. I do apologise. May we go back to -- well, no. I'll withdraw the question altogether. Thank you. That completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, we did -- our apologies to the interpreters. We did our best to finish your testimony today. You obviously have every reason to complain that we tired you out. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, my colleagues Judge Kwon, Judge Prost, and Judge Stole, I wish to thank you for having been kind enough not only to come with us but to -- to come to give testimony in this case but also to be patient with us, and on behalf of everyone here I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to thank all of those in the courtroom who have followed everything I've been saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's move to documents now. Which one is -- all right. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have a list, but I will double-check this list and eventually ask to tendering for next sitting date, is day after tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thursday. All right. Okay then that gives us time with your indulgence to go through some pending issues. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My colleagues and I have gone through the motion already, and since we have very limited time within which to decide the issue in case we grant it, we would like you to possibly respond to it by the end of this week. The main points raised in that motion is the relevance of his testimony and also his health condition, but as I understand it the accompanying or supporting documents as to his health need to be translated. That requires time, and as they are, they are not very much legible. We would like you to come back to us with your response by the end of the week. Do you think that would be possible, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sure it is, though this is beginning to mount up on us, all of these last minute issues without exhibits, without statements. We are making a filing on this issue in particular that I was hoping to get yesterday, but it will be filed today, but this is beginning to really make it difficult to be prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not only to you, but also to us and our staff, but I hope that this is only transient, transitory, brought about by the fact that the Beara Defence team has been faced with a different schedule that they may have had in mind until a few days ago. So let's try to keep calm, all of us, and also try to be reasonable, and I'm sure that you are all capable of this. So if you can, please, try to come back to us with a response by the end of Friday. Now, one moment because I have other things to -- yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For example, there was a previous motion by the same Defence team for the hearing of the testimony of Osman Dizdarevic to be heard by video conference link. We had encouraged you to come to some sort of an arrangement or agreement between you. We haven't had a feedback from either of you, so to date we don't know whether we are going to hear the testimony of this gentleman at all or that's going to be by video conference link because we haven't decided that pending information from you, or whether his testimony will be provided in some other format. At the same time, he is not listed in the immediate list of Beara team witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe, though I'm -- could be mistaken, but I'm pretty sure that's a fellow that Mr. Ostojic and I spoke about, and he clarified that this was a man that would just speak about his treatment as a prisoner in 1993 or 1992, and we said if that's the case and if the statement reflects that when we get it, then we don't have a problem, him being 92 bis, and so we don't need any videolink, and I think that's the same person, and so we should be able to 92 bis that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are definitely talking about the same person, yes. Mr. Ostojic, do you have anything to say about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We've learned from witnesses, obviously their health condition may have changed over the course of the last month or two, so when we called them we were advised of his poor health. We are still trying to contact him to see exactly what his health condition is like. We will in the alternative either present his testimony pursuant to 92 bis or to simply withdraw the witness, and I communicated that with my learned friend several days ago actually, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. There was -- yesterday we had an indication that the Prosecution was to make or was intending to make a filing either yesterday. Subsequently, it appeared that it would happen today, that being the Prosecution's response to the supplemental motion by the Beara team for leave to amend the 62 ter list, which was filed on the 2nd of July. Can you update us on that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As you know, I left early yesterday and -- but I'm told in consultations with Mr. Thayer and Mr. Nichols that that's going to be filed today. I haven't spoken to them yet today about it, but I'm convinced that it should come in today, and I of course will let you know if there's been some significant issue, but it should be today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then there were two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I have something along those lines, as well, to clear something up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You may recall the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There were two witnesses, Witness number 98 and Witness number 11 -- I forgot his number now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it was 105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, something like that, I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know we resolved that. I don't remember how. Maybe Mr. Ostojic can help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We resolved that as reflected in the notice of filing that the Prosecution does not object to their 92 bis statements coming into evidence. We have an e-mail to that effect, and also we had verbally spoke about it, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had indication but of course since we will be handing down a bitten decision, we need to have your position publicly stated either in writing or orally we are happy with an oral statement to that effect in this case it has to come from the Prosecution. We didn't have it until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes you are correct it's 98 and 105.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes I agree with Mr. Ostojic that was one of the many things we've been speaking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think I have covered all the pending issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one small, well, one issue that I think is important to clear up, Mr. President. You may recall during the testimony on I guess it was 30 June of the ICMP Defence or the DNA Defence expert there was use of an ICMP document called a tracking chart that had the various summaries of their results and Judge Kwon asked why this need today be in private session and we did check that and we've requested ICMP and they were able to say that it was not a problem for them if that is now in open session. So we would request that that be lifted.
